headline: Mitchell Stone sees Rubicon Water (RWL) as oversold at a $30m market cap, expecting a positive earnings surprise as US government spending resumes
reasoning: Stone identifies Rubicon Water, which builds intelligent irrigation control hardware and software to automate open-channel water delivery, as a structural beneficiary of water scarcity given that agriculture accounts for 70% of freshwater withdrawal and 60% of that is lost to inefficient delivery. The share price has been heavily sold off over recent years to a point Stone believes it is oversold, with a market cap of only $30 million. A weak first-half result was attributed to US government shutdowns, which have since ended, and Stone expects the full-year results (reporting on Monday) to be strong and surprise to the upside. He also notes the CEO of UBS Australia holds 18% of the company and has invested around $6 million of personal capital, which he takes as a positive signal. He flags the stock is very thinly traded and patience will be required.
quote: So there's a stock that I'm looking at at the moment called the tickers RW, L, Rubicon Water. They build intelligent irrigation control tech which is hardware and software to automate the whole thing. This company's been around for around 30 years, so it's quite an established business. As you can see, the the share price has been belted over the past couple of years, but to a point where I believe that it's been oversold. The market cap is just $30 million at the moment. Um, in terms of timing, they report on Monday, and I think that the the market has been too pessimistic. They had a weak, really weak first half of the year. That was thanks to government shutdowns over in the US and, um, the US government's back up online and spending left, right and centre. So I dare say that the the full year results will be quite good.

headline: Mitchell Stone flags structural water scarcity opportunity driven by inefficient agricultural irrigation, with AI and data centre buildout compounding demand
reasoning: Stone highlights that agriculture accounts for 70% of global freshwater withdrawal and 60% of that is lost through inefficient open-channel delivery systems with no real-time control, leading to seepage, evaporation, and over-delivery. The drying up of the Colorado River in the US is cited as a recent example of growing scarcity pressures. Data centres add incremental demand pressure on water resources. He sees this as a structural opportunity for irrigation technology companies.
quote: So big issues with water. Um, we saw that in the US with the Colorado River drying up last year. The issue is that agriculture accounts for 70% of freshwater withdrawal. Now, 60% of that is lost to inefficient delivery. I'm talking about open channel systems with no real time control. That leads to huge loss volumes of seepage, evaporation and over delivery.

headline: Mitchell Stone bullish on copper due to surging demand from China's infrastructure program and AI buildout, with supply unable to keep pace
reasoning: Stone notes copper prices have risen from around 620 to 650 in a month and shows no sign of topping. China's six networks infrastructure program — a five-year, $4 trillion spend from 2026 to 2030 on electricity grids, telco, and water — is a major demand driver alongside data centres. On the supply side, major producing countries like Chile are seeing lower output, and new mines take 10–15 years to come online, meaning no near-term supply relief. Stone says he cannot see copper prices topping in the short term.
quote: The price of copper just doesn't want to go down does it? You see little dips along the journey. Then it picks back up again. But a month ago, when I was in the studios, I think copper was about 620. Now it's up to 650. Yeah, we did touch on the data centers using a tremendous amount of copper, but just a lot of it's coming from from China. You know, they've announced the six networks infrastructure program. That's a five year program starting from 2026 to end of 2030. They're going to spend $4 trillion on that, building out their electricity grids and telco and water systems, really getting their, their, um, economy and their infrastructure up to date for the, um, the AI generation. So, yeah, huge, huge demand and supply is, is falling lower output from the major countries like Chile at the moment.

headline: Mitchell Stone flags Carbon XT as a deeply undervalued ASX micro-cap benefiting from surging activated carbon demand driven by US PFAS remediation mandates.
reasoning: The US EPA has mandated water utility companies reduce PFAS levels to four parts per trillion by 2029, and activated carbon is currently the only scalable solution. Carbon XT is the only ASX-listed producer of activated carbon, operating two facilities in the US (Minnesota and Georgia), with a third facility — converted from an old power station via a 50/50 JV — expected to come online within months and produce around 10,000 tons per year. Production costs are approximately $2,000 per ton against a selling price of ~$4,000, giving healthy margins. Despite being cash-flow positive this year, the company's $30 million market cap reflects near-zero market awareness. Smart operators including Bronte Capital's Simon Maher and Pure Asset Management have been quietly accumulating shares, suggesting the market mispricing is temporary.
quote: There's only one ASX company that I know of that produces activated carbon. It's a company called Carbon XT, ASX CG one. It's a micro cap $30 million market cap. And there's just no awareness about this company. It's been around for a while, producing for over ten years... They can't keep up with business. So what they've recently done is converted an old power station via a 5050 JV to produce this activated carbon. And that's going to be a really exciting milestone for this company. To put things into perspective, let's talk dollar figures. It costs them about $2,000 a ton to make this stuff. And they sell it for about 4000. So healthy margins. And when this new facility comes online very soon I'm expecting within the next few months this new facility should produce somewhere around 10,000 tons per year... This will be a cash flow positive business this year. You look at their two largest shareholders, SLB PT limited, which more or less is a proxy for Bronte Capital, Simon Maher, who manages billions and Pure Asset Management. There's some smart operators. They've been quietly buying, buying, buying and they've been soaking up all of the selling recently. I just think it's only a matter of time before the market catches on.
episode_title: Two ASX small caps with long-term potential

headline: US EPA PFAS mandate by 2029 creating massive structural demand for activated carbon as the only scalable remediation solution.
reasoning: The US EPA has enforced regulations requiring water utility companies to reduce PFAS forever chemical levels to four parts per trillion by 2029 — equivalent to four drops in 20 Olympic-sized swimming pools. PFAS is linked to thyroid cancer and other cancers and accumulates in the human body without breaking down. Activated carbon is currently the only technology capable of filtering PFAS at scale, and demand is materially outstripping supply with no futures market or price transparency, making it an opaque but structurally favourable market.
quote: The US EPA is actually enforced these water utility companies by 2029 that they need to reduce the levels of forever chemicals and PFAS down to four parts per trillion by 2029. And to put that into perspective. That's like four drops in 20 Olympic sized swimming pools. So yeah, big, big problem in America right now. They need to reduce it. And the only way to do that currently on scale is by filtering the water, by using what's called activated carbon... The overall trend of activated carbon is certainly heading in the right direction. The demand is very much outstripping supply currently.
